articles.title: Ekurhuleni killings: What we know after bodies of 12 women found in South Africa
articles.summary: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa says the murders are a "stain on our national conscience".
articles.body:
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.

The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.

Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.

The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.

Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.

Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.

Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.

The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.

Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.

Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.

Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.

No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.

Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.

Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.

Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.

Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.

Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.

The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.

Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.

She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.

The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.

According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.

The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.

The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.

This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.

A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.

The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.

The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.

The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.

Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.

Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.

Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.

While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.

The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.

It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.

President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".

South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.

South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.

Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

articles.title: Slipknot reveal world tour with Marilyn Manson as support act
articles.summary: The heavy metal band will be joined by the US rock musician during their London show.
articles.body:
Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act.

The eight-piece group, known for performing in masks, will be joined by the US rock musician during their shows at London's Wembley Stadium and multiple dates of the South American leg of the tour.

Some fans have reacted angrily to the news and said they will not attend the shows over past sexual abuse accusations against the 57-year-old.

Manson, real name Brian Warner, has always strongly denied any allegations against him.

Thousands of fans replied to an Instagram post featuring the line-up for the London gigs, which also includes metalcore band Hatebreed.

While some posts expressed excitement at the support acts, many were critical of Manson's presence on the bill, describing it as "disappointing".

Others, who described themselves as long-time Slipknot fans, said they would not buy tickets for the show in protest at his appearance.

One wrote: "Would've loved to see this but there's literally nothing you could do to get my cash in Manson's pockets."

Another added the announcement was "such a disappointment" and they would not be attending.

However, others disagreed, with one pointing out the two acts have a "huge fanbase overlap" and describing Manson as a "perfect support act".

Manson was publicly accused of abuse by actress Evan Rachel Wood , who was in a three-year relationship with the singer from 2007.

Posting in 2021, she alleged he "horrifically abused" and "manipulated" her and said she had spoken out to warn others about "a dangerous man".

Manson said the claims were "horrible distortions of reality" and his "intimate relationships had always been entirely consensual".

Several other women came forward on social media at the time with similar statements accusing Manson of abuse.

Wood featured in a 2022 documentary series, Phoenix Rising, which focused on her allegations against Manson.

He sued Wood and another woman for defamation, accusing them of impersonating FBI agents and forging federal documents.

A judge dismissed some of Manson's claims, and he eventually settled the case and agreed to pay Woods' legal fees in 2024.

Last year, prosecutors in Los Angeles said they would not bring criminal charges against Manson after a four-year investigation into accusations of domestic abuse and sexual assault involving multiple women.

The district attorney's office said the domestic abuse charges fell "outside of the statute of limitations" and it was unable to "prove charges of sexual assault beyond a reasonable doubt."

articles.title: Photos: Russian drone strikes pound civilian targets across Kyiv
articles.summary: Ukraine condemns Russian targeting of civilians as strikes kill seven and injure dozens across Kyiv.
articles.body:
Russian drones have struck Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in the historic centre of Kyiv, as Moscow’s forces continue to pound the capital around the clock.

Ukrainian officials reported that at least seven people were killed and more than 80 wounded on Monday as Russian strikes hit apartment blocks, offices, petrol stations, data centres and cultural sites.

In Kyiv, a woman died and several people were injured when a high-speed drone smashed into the academy building near the German embassy and key government institutions.

Staff were seen escaping down firefighters’ ladders as flames engulfed part of the structure. Mayor Vitali Klitschko condemned the strikes as “pure terror” aimed at disrupting normal life and breaking civilian morale.

Elsewhere, three people were killed in a strike on an office centre in Dnipro, while dozens were wounded in attacks on Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa.

Moscow says it is targeting military-related sites, but Ukraine accuses Russia of systematic attacks on civilians and infrastructure to cripple its economy and force concessions in stalled peace efforts to end the two countries’ four-and-a-half-year war.

articles.title: Man accused of holding woman captive in a Massachusetts attic for six weeks
articles.summary: A 29-year-old man is accused of kidnapping and sexually trafficking a woman who prosecutors said was held for six weeks in the unfinished attic of a home in Malden, Massachusetts, before the property owner discovered her and called police.
articles.body: A 29-year-old man is accused of kidnapping and sexually trafficking a woman who prosecutors said was held for six weeks in the unfinished attic of a home in Malden, Massachusetts, before the property owner discovered her and called police. Jordende Pierre is facing charges including trafficking a person for sexual servitude, kidnapping and indecent assault and battery on a person 14 or older. Prosecutors said the woman was found Sunday naked and malnourished on a mat in the attic of a multifamily home on Summer Street. “She clearly had not eaten, she was dirty. She was living, essentially, in squalor in this attic area,” Middlesex County Assistant District Attorney Jacob McCrindle said in court. Authorities said a five-gallon bucket containing urine was found near the woman. According to prosecutors, Pierre met the woman through a dating app and brought her to the Malden home about six weeks before she was discovered. The woman, who prosecutors said struggled with substance abuse, was allegedly given drugs while at the home. Prosecutors allege Pierre sexually assaulted her and forced her to have sexual encounters with other men who came to the property. “The defendant would arrange for those dates,” McCrindle said. Prosecutors also described how Pierre allegedly prevented the woman from leaving the attic. “The door handle in this attic area, it could be removed, and the defendant would remove that door handle so that she could not leave,” McCrindle said. Property owner and landlord Qing Sun told NBC Boston exclusively that she and her husband went to the Summer Street property Sunday because of a water leak. Sun lives offsite, but manages the units at the property. She said tenants initially prevented the couple from accessing certain rooms while they were trying to determine where the water problem was coming from. The couple eventually made their way to the attic, where Sun said they discovered the woman and a man, who ran past them. That’s when they called 911. “It’s a disturbing situation,” Sun said, adding that she was also relieved to find out what was going on. Police arrived and removed the woman from the property. Sun said Pierre was not one of her tenants and that she had no knowledge of anyone living in the attic. “This guy is not on the list. I’m not aware this guy is living there,” Sun said. “And I’m not aware anybody living in the attic. Nobody’s supposed to live there.” Pierre was not arrested until Thursday, when multiple law enforcement agencies, including Malden police, the FBI and U.S. Marshals, participated in an operation to take him into custody. “I’m very happy to be able to help this young girl get back to her family,” Sun said. The allegations stunned people living near the Summer Street property, although some neighbors said the house had drawn attention before. One neighbor described the home as “Frankenstein’s home.” “We’ve heard rumors about that house in the past,” neighbor Tarra Sewell said. “I would never, ever imagine something happening so close to my home ... That’s really, really scary.” Another neighbor described the people coming and going from the property as “kind of a rotating cast of characters,” saying neighbors did not always know who lived there. Neighbors also described parties and loud music at the property, including on weeknights, and said police had previously responded following complaints. One neighbor said seeing the large law enforcement presence during Pierre’s arrest made the allegations even more unsettling. “There were a huge force of police. It sounds like they were very coordinated and organized,” neighbor Kirby Tang said. Tang said it was painful knowing the woman had allegedly been held so close to surrounding homes without neighbors realizing what was happening. “I just feel sorry for her; like, she was 500 feet away and we couldn’t do anything,” Tang said. “Because we didn’t hear anything.” Sun said she is checking the property nearly every week now and hopes what happened will encourage others to pay closer attention to their surroundings and report suspicious activity. Pierre also has an open assault and battery with a dangerous weapon case in Somerville and had been out on bail. He’s now being held until his next court hearing for the Malden case on Oct. 6. Police have not ruled out additional arrests in the Summer Street investigation.

articles.title: Dan Dakich calls Chris Simms' apology over Dante Moore slide analysis 'soft a-- bulls--t'
articles.summary: Chris Simms apologized after his halftime analysis of the Dante Moore "dirty hit" debate, but Dan Dakich says the apology was wildly unnecessary.
articles.body: After Oregon quarterback Dante Moore took a brutal hit following an attempt to slide after a first down on Saturday against USC, it started one of the most fiery debates this college football season. Many claimed it was a "dirty hit", including CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore, Heisman Trophy winner Robert Griffin III, and SEC Nation personality Chase Daniel who went as far as calling it the dirtiest hit I've ever seen. It seemed the only cool, calm, collected, and informed take came from NBC Sports' personality and former NFL quarterback, Chris Simms. During halftime, Simms was asked to put himself in Moore's shoes and provide his take based on experience. After explaining that it was a "Debbie Downer moment" because no one likes to see someone get hurt and carted off the field. Fans and teams want to play at full strength. Then he shared something personal his dad told him in college after being announced as the starting quarterback for the University of Texas, "Christopher, when you get out there running around, make sure you get down in time, and don't take any big hits." Simms went on to say after explaining how defenders are essentially foaming at the mouth waiting for the chance to hit the QB in the open field, "You want to slide in plenty of time to keep your body safe." It was an informed, common sense statement, based on his unique, relevant experience, but that didn't sit well with many Oregon and college football fans outraged online. OREGON DUCKS QB DANTE MOORE CARTED OFF THE FIELD AFTER A VICIOUS HIT TO THE HEAD AGAINST USC Simms further analyzed the incident by explaining how hard the game is one defensive players nowadays. "You have to have a soft spot in your heart for defenders right now," Simm stated. "You gotta think, Dante Moore is 6'3" 220 pounds, he's running at you, the defender [Desman] Stephens is bracing himself, getting ready to get low to make the tackle, so yes, you as a defender, have to know in this day and age that you have to be careful with the quarterback. But I would also say, Dante Moore slide very late, and kind of put the defender in a no win situation." Again, it was informed analysis of a play that, in my opinion, too many people were framing in an unfair light, making Stephens out as a head hunter and Moore as an innocent victim that "clearly gave himself up" as Steratore claimed. Simms then took to social media Sunday and apologized to "all college football fans" saying, "I clearly did not show enough sympathy for the situation." Following an apology to Oregon Ducks fans, and head coach Dan Lanning, Simms said, "I mishandled the situation and I was wrong. I'm sorry for that." Dont @ Me host Dan Dakich, as do I, felt that apology was wildly unnecessary. Dakich unloaded on Simms claim that he wasn't sympathetic enough saying, "Bulls–t! You're not there to show sympathy. You're there to explain the situation based on your experience." "I don't know why that's a problem," Dakich said. "I think Chris Simms is absolutely right here," while reacting to Simms analysis of the hit on Moore. "This was a quarterback going full speed and slide late," Dakich stated, echoing Simms initial analysis. A big issue within this incident was how Stephens reacted following the hit, which left Moore motionless on the field, leading to the Oregon QB being carted off the field. He was seen taunting, laughing, dapping up his teammates, and more unsportsmanlike conduct. Dakich addressed that saying, "All you have to say is that guy is an idiot and he should be suspended." Simms actually scolded Stephens at halftime for his antics saying, "That was a bad look for USC." "There's no reason for this apology. This is just soft a– bulls–t by Chris Simms," Dakich said definitively. NEW RESEARCH FINDS 1 IN 4 NFL PLAYERS COULD DEVELOP CTE IN THEIR LIFETIME: 'SHOULD BE A CALL TO ACTION' Stephens has since been suspended one game by USC for his reaction following the brutal hit on Moore. "He understands his mistake, accepts the consequences of his actions and will learn from this," Trojans head coach Lincoln Riley said. "The entire Trojan Family wishes Dante a full recovery, and we send our best regards to him and his family." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: Trump made the right decision to reject Iran’s offer
articles.summary: The US president has denied Tehran the opportunity to use the US midterm elections as a pressure point.
articles.body:
The Strait of Hormuz remains the most perilous choke point on the global map as Iran continues to disrupt traffic by attacking vessels. A recent proposal by the Islamic Republic to open the waterway within seven days raised hopes that the situation could go back to normal. United States President Donald Trump, however, rejected the offer.

To understand the strategic calculus behind his high-stakes decision, one must look beyond the immediate tactical noise and peer into the deeper logic of deterrence.

On its surface, the rejection of a temporary truce in the world’s most vital energy corridor appears to be a reckless gamble – a provocation inviting the very conflagration the West seeks to avoid. But viewed through the lens of cold realism, the rejection was not only a calculated necessity; it was the right decision.

The Iranian regime’s proposal was a classic exercise in asymmetric diplomacy. It offered a brief window of stability, a transactional pause, in exchange for what would have amounted to a de facto relaxation of American pressure. To accept such terms would have meant embracing the delusional belief that a terrorist power can be bribed into good behaviour by accepting its terms of engagement.

Had Washington accepted, it would have validated Iran’s self-assumed right to turn the spigot of global commerce on and off at will. By flatly rejecting the offer, Trump signalled that freedom of navigation is not a chip to be bartered in a week-long bazaar, but an absolute, non-negotiable prerequisite of international order.

The timing of this gambit – on the eve of the critical midterm elections – has naturally drawn the ire of the domestic political class. Critics argue that risking an energy crisis and a subsequent spike in oil prices weeks before Americans head to the ballot box is an act of political self-immolation. This view, while superficially plausible, misunderstands both the nature of the electorate and the psychology of our adversaries.

The Iranians chose this moment to put forward their proposal precisely because of the midterm elections. They are sophisticated observers of American domestic politics. They calculated that an administration facing an electoral test would be paralysed by the fear of rising fuel prices and would eagerly grasp at any diplomatic lifeline, however flimsy, to keep the peace until November.

Had Trump capitulated to save Republicans a few points at the polls, he would have handed Iran a profound psychological victory. He would have demonstrated that American foreign policy is subservient to the domestic election calendar – a vulnerability that every autocracy from Moscow to Beijing would immediately exploit.

By taking the gamble before the midterm elections, Trump has turned the tables. He has demonstrated that his administration is willing to absorb short-term political pain in pursuit of long-term strategic clarity. This is the essence of credible deterrence.

Deterrence is not merely a function of military hardware; it is a function of perceived will. When an adversary believes you are too weak, too compromised, or too worried about the next election cycle to defend your core interests, deterrence fails. By rejecting the seven-day proposal, the Trump administration proved it could not be blackmailed by the electoral calendar.

Trump’s decision reflects a sophisticated understanding of the regime in Tehran. The Islamic Republic is currently facing an acute internal economic crisis, a direct consequence of the sustained American maximum-pressure campaign.

The seven-day proposal was not a gesture of Iranian confidence; it was a sign of desperation disguised as a diplomatic overture. It was an attempt to buy breathing room, fragment the expanding international coalition against Tehran and project an image of being in control to its own restive population.

To grant Iran that reprieve would have been to throw a lifeline to an antagonist regime on the ropes. Clearly, this offer was only made because US strategy is working and Iran’s economy is cratering.

History teaches us that truces with terrorist regimes are rarely precursors to permanent peace; they are merely opportunities for the aggressor to rearm, recalibrate and choose the next moment of confrontation on more favourable terms. A short-term guarantee of open shipping lanes implied that any day, the threat could return, magnified by the legitimacy Washington would have afforded to Iran’s leverage.

The critics who cry havoc at this decision are the heirs of the foreign policy establishment that spent decades managing decline through endless, inconclusive and failed negotiations. They prefer the comfortable fiction of a temporary deal to the hard reality of a sustained geopolitical contest.

President Trump’s gamble is risky, yes. The potential for miscalculation in the narrow waters of the Gulf is always present. But the risk of inaction, or of a pliant accommodation, is far greater.

By holding the line, the administration has reaffirmed a foundational principle of US global stewardship: the US will not permit rogue states to hold the global economy hostage.

The rejection of the Iranian proposal is the correct path because it chooses clarity of American resolve over partisan political convenience. It signals to the regime in Iran that its leverage is artificial and its economic isolation is permanent unless its behaviour changes.

This November, American voters will decide the composition of the US Congress based on a multitude of domestic and foreign policy factors. But on the global stage, Trump remains steadfast by demonstrating that principle trumps political expediency.

articles.summary: The threatened proposal aims to protect US consumers from rising costs, but it could trigger major economic waves if it were to happen.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said he would back a ban on diesel producers selling overseas as surging fuel prices hit drivers ahead of the midterm elections.

Diesel prices are hovering near a record $6.45 per gallon on average, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), due to the ongoing US-Israel war with Iran and tight global supplies.

Trump and his backers say a US diesel export ban would protect domestic consumers from those rising costs, but experts say it could trigger major economic waves both at home and across the world if it were to happen.

How much diesel does the US produce and export?

The US is one of the world's leading energy producers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels of diesel every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).

Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that daily output. Refiners export the remaining1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market.

Between 60% and 70% of this exported fuel goes to Latin America. Nations like Mexico, Brazil, Chile, and Ecuador depend heavily on American shipments to power their transport, farming, and factory sectors.

Significant volumes also head across the Atlantic to European countries like France, the Netherlands, and the UK, as buyers search for alternatives to Middle Eastern supplies.

What has happened to diesel prices in the US and abroad?

US diesel prices have climbed to a record high of over $6.50 per gallon – up nearly 70% year-on-year.

The spike has been driven by broader energy market shocks tied to ongoing conflict with Iran , which has restricted critical shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway south of Iran through which one fifth of the world's oil and gas usually flows.

Diesel primarily fuels commercial vehicles in the US – such as freight trucks, farm machinery, and cargo trains – which are used for transporting goods and construction.

This means higher diesel prices can drive up the price of food, building projects, and many other things.

Outside the US, diesel is used in both commercial and consumer vehicles, but the effects of higher prices are similar.

In the UK, diesel prices at the pump have hit an all-time high , prompting warnings about logistics costs and household budgets.

UK Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News that the UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential diesel export ban and has started preparing for it.

Meanwhile, in France and across continental Europe, governments are struggling with similar cost-of-living pressures because of rising fuel prices.

What has Trump said, and what is his argument?

Trump suggested over the weekend that restricting or outright banning US diesel exports could keep fuel in the domestic market and drive down prices for American consumers.

The president said on Sunday that the administration was "thinking about it very seriously".

His comments mirror remarks made on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, where he stated that he had called to "not send out the diesel".

Trump argues that keeping those extra barrels in the US would lower pump prices, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections.

Supporters, including key Republican lawmakers like Congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Senator Dan Sullivan, view the strategy as an effective way to shield the domestic economy from foreign shocks, arguing that American energy should serve American workers first.

What would an export ban mean for the US and the rest of the world?

For the US economy, a ban could deliver short-term relief at the pump by flooding the domestic market with excess supply.

However, energy analysts warn it could backfire.

David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, notes that cutting off American supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket.

That would push up global freight, food, and industrial costs, ultimately "feeding inflation back into the global economy".

"At a stroke, the US's reputation as a reliable supplier of energy to the world would be shot," Fyfe added.

Removing more than a million barrels of daily American supply would trigger a fierce bidding war among importing nations in Latin America and Europe.

Sarah Raffoul, analytics manager at Argus Media, noted that while higher international prices would eventually curb demand, the immediate gap would severely strain trade relationships and accelerate global inflation.

articles.title: Iran under scrutiny after plot foiled near UK base used by US military
articles.summary: Experts suspect an Iran link after five were allegedly arrested with explosives near a U.K. U.S. military base. Russia and Islamic terrorists are also under scrutiny.
articles.body: Just days after left-wing British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband shook hands with the Islamic Republic of Iran’s top diplomat at the United Nations, U.K. authorities arrested five men with possible links to Tehran who allegedly sought to bomb a military base in Fairford used by American forces. Armed officers arrested the five suspected terrorists who were traveling in three vans reportedly packed with explosive material. The authorities seized the five British nationals and the vans a mere 350 yards from the military base, which is used by the U.S. Army to launch air strikes against military targets in Iran. Speaking from London on Monday, Nile Gardiner, the director of the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital, "I think it is highly likely it was an Iranian orchestrated attack. It is stunning that they have released terrorist suspects on bail. It strikes me as entirely insane. The suspects appear to be Muslim Islamists, judging by the picture." BRITAIN INTRODUCES SWEEPING NEW POWERS TO TARGET FOREIGN STATE-LINKED GROUPS INCLUDING IRAN'S IRGC Gardiner said, "The British government is on a full appeasement drive toward Tehran. We saw that with Ed Miliband meeting with the Iranian foreign minister at the U.N. General Assembly. The U.K. does not want to get involved in the U.S.-led war against Tehran." He said the current government is a "socialist appeasement-minded British administration that is incredibly weak on defense and national security." The United States and Israel launched a joint military campaign on Feb. 28 to knock out Iran's nuclear weapons and missile systems. A source familiar with the Fairford investigation had previously ⁠told Reuters that an Iranian-linked motive was considered the most likely, although a Russian sabotage operation or an Islamist plot were also being looked at as possibilities. When President Donald Trump was asked if the bomb plot was linked to Iran’s regime, he said on Monday that "It might be, but I will tell you, I would have said, don't let them have bail. Cashless bail. I wonder, is it cashless bail? I guess that was one of the problems that we had, which started the whole mess of crime. And we're ending cashless bail." He continued that "But over there, I'm surprised that they released them. I wouldn't have done that. Look, they've been very good. They worked with us very closely. We know everything about them. We would not have released them." On Sunday, Trump said the suspects were "looking to do big damage." He added, "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them." A spokesperson for Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that "when asked whether President Trump’s comments were accurate, the Prime Minister’s official spokesperson said the Defence Secretary had been asked about them on the morning round and referred journalists to his words. He said the investigation was ongoing, and it would not be appropriate to comment further." EUROPE WILL ONE DAY THANK TRUMP FOR 'SHAKING' IT OUT OF ITS 'COMPLACENCY': UK DEFENSE CHIEF The U.S. and U.K.-designated terrorist movement, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), put the British government on notice in July that military installations used to attack Iran are legitimate targets for retaliation. Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which tracks Iran’s terrorist and spycraft activities in the United Kingdom, told Fox News Digital, "I believe Iran would have a motive for such a plot. This is because in July, authorities in Cyprus arrested a man accused of spying for Iran at RAF [Royal Air Force] Akrotiri. Iranian officials and media have also pointed to RAF Fairford specifically, dubbing it ‘an important matter for our self-defense’ amid Operation Epic Fury." IRAN EXPERT BRANDS ISLAMIC CENTER OF ENGLAND IRAN'S 'UK OFFICE,' URGES IMMEDIATE CLOSURE Brodsky added, "Iran has a long history of launching terror plots in the U.K., via its Intelligence Ministry and the IRGC. It has long used criminal gangs as proxies to mask its involvement. So I suspect U.K. authorities are probing these angles as part of the investigation." The U.K.’s Counterterrorism Policing Office said the five suspects were detained on suspicion of offenses under the Explosives Act and preparation of a terrorist act contrary to Section 5 of the Terrorism Act. Vicki Evans, counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator, deputy assistant commissioner, said, "This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation, involving local and national policing, the MOD, and local agencies, who are working together to progress the investigation and support for the community." Evans added, "I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised." According to an X post by the Iranian regime’s embassy in London, "The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base." The Iranian Embassy added "The Circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK. The Islamic Republic of Iran reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives." Barak Seener, senior fellow at the London-based Henry Jackson Society, told Fox News Digital, "The British government has no sense of how to prioritize its national security interests. While British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi at the U.N. that the United Kingdom will not tolerate intimidation, threats, or hostile activity on British soil, he was sure to take a friendly picture with him, while purposely avoiding meeting any Israeli representative." He added, "Similarly, at the Labor Party conference, Ed Miliband spent 15 seconds on Iran, and close to four minutes on Israel. This has led to an environment in which a suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford could take place." A spokesperson for the British government told Fox News Digital, "The police have issued a statement this afternoon from the head of CTP. We don’t have any further comment at this early stage." With respect to the Fox News Digital press query about Miliband's meeting with Araghchi at the U.N., the British government spokesperson sent Fox News Digital a readout of the meeting, "The Foreign Secretary told Araghchi that Iran should choose de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war. He underlined the importance of restoring freedom of navigation and the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, stressing the impact continued disruption has on global security and economic stability. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The Foreign Secretary reiterated the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community. The Foreign Secretary made clear that Britain will not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil and set out the measures the Government has taken in response. He also raised the ongoing detention of Craig and Lindsay Foreman, repeating the UK's call for their immediate release and stressing that their welfare remains a priority for the Government." Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Deshaun Watson is beginning to craft one of the most improbable comeback stories in sports history
articles.summary: This season, Deshaun Watson's 104.1 passer rating nearly matches MVP frontrunner Josh Allen's as the Cleveland Browns sit at 2-1 in the AFC North race.
articles.body: Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson has already had one of the more unusual careers in modern NFL history. After an acclaimed college career at Clemson, the Houston Texans drafted him 12th overall in 2017, two picks after the Kansas City Chiefs selected Patrick Mahomes. Unlike Mahomes, Watson played early in his rookie season. Almost immediately, he looked like a phenomenon. That October, his first full month as a starter, Watson threw 16 touchdowns, setting the NFL record for touchdown passes by a rookie in a calendar month. He was named AFC Offensive Player of the Month. Watson was an MVP candidate in just his first season. Then, on Nov. 2, 2017, he tore his ACL on a non-contact play during practice, ending his season. He returned the following year and established himself as a solid franchise quarterback. By his fourth season as a starter, he had recaptured much of his rookie form. Despite the Texans winning just four games in 2020, Watson led the NFL in passing yards (4,823), completion percentage (70.2%), and passer rating (112.4). By the end of that season, there was a growing perception that Watson had moved past Josh Allen and Lamar Jackson as the one true rival to Mahomes, who had already won one Super Bowl and appeared in another. At the time, Watson said he envisioned himself and Mahomes as the "next Tom Brady and Peyton Manning." He was not alone. Colin Cowherd, Michael Vick, Jason Whitlock, Stephen A. Smith, Max Kellerman, and ProFootballTalk also made the comparison. Then his career unraveled. That offseason, 27 women filed civil lawsuits accusing Watson of sexual misconduct and assault during massage therapy appointments. The Texans sat him for the entire 2021 season. The Browns traded for him the following year, sending Houston three first-round picks. Cleveland and Watson then agreed to an unprecedented five-year, $230 million fully guaranteed contract, the largest guaranteed deal in NFL history at the time. Watson was suspended for six regular-season games to start the 2022 season by arbitrator Sue L. Robinson as a result of the sexual misconduct allegations. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE He made his Browns debut later that season and struggled. The struggles continued the following year, and injuries ensued. From 2022 through 2025, Watson played in just 19 games. He suffered two Achilles ruptures in that span. Statistically, he was among the worst quarterbacks in the entire NFL. In one of the more stunning public acknowledgments by an NFL owner, Browns owner Jimmy Haslam acknowledged that trading for Watson was a mistake that set the franchise back years. "We took a big swing and miss with Deshaun," Jimmy Haslam told reporters in 2025. "We thought we had the quarterback, we didn't and we gave up a lot of draft picks to get him. So we've got to dig ourselves out of that hole. (It) was an entire organization decision and it ends with Dee and I, so hold us accountable." Despite the admission, Watson remained on the roster. Ahead of this season, disdain for Watson’s play and character united nearly every corner of sports media. Between the scandal, the contract, the performance, and the attitude, Watson had become perhaps the most disliked athlete in American sports. Some outlets made that case. Few athletes can put Jemele Hill and Clay Travis on the same side of an argument. Watson did. The industry clamored for the Browns to start Shedeur Sanders before opening day. Browns fans agreed, even booing Watson as he walked onto the field during a preseason game. Head coach Todd Monken received fierce backlash after he named Watson the starter. ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky said Browns fans should consider skipping home games in protest. "I don't think they can have Deshaun Watson on the team after that interaction," Orlovsky said. "And, if they somehow come out today and name Deshaun Watson their starting quarterback, if I was a Browns fan, I wouldn't go to the game. You cannot handle a press conference that way, given the circumstances of what has transpired after they gave you $230-plus, $250 million guaranteed, and the lack of performance and availability has shown itself." Betting markets posted odds before the season not on whether the Browns would bench Watson, but when. DESHAUN WATSON GOES FROM CLEVELAND VILLIAN TO HERO IN BROWNS UPSET WIN, AS HOME CROWD TURNS JEERS INTO CHEERS Through three weeks, Watson’s career is undergoing yet another strange shift in public perception. The Browns are 2-1, in a four-way tie in the AFC North. Watson has played well. More importantly, he has played well in the clutch in back-to-back weeks. For comparison, his 104.1 passer rating is nearly identical to MVP frontrunner Josh Allen’s. Suddenly, Watson has supporters again. He has fans. In one of the biggest early-season upsets, Browns fans chanted "Let’s go Watson" after he led the team to victory in the final minutes against Carolina. His general manager greeted him in the tunnel with a hug. Just as the previous stage of Watson’s career united unlikely voices in opposition, his budding comeback has done the same in reverse. Get this: both Jason Whitlock and Stephen A. Smith praised Watson for his performance Sunday. Former coach Rex Ryan said Watson "looks like" he did in Houston for the first time since the scandal. Watson may never be a sympathetic figure. The allegations against him suggest a pattern of poor conduct, even if some details are disputed. At 31, coming off two Achilles tears, Watson is unlikely to fulfill the prediction that he would become the Peyton Manning to Mahomes’ Tom Brady. But a month ago, his career looked as if it was nearing an end, as if the Browns wants him to prove one final time he was unplayable. That's certainly how the media and fans interpreted his role this season. He has since responded, finally making something of a second chance that all players would receive. Case in point: Justin Tucker, who faced similar allegations and has not returned since. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Suddenly, Watson is no longer merely the scandal-stained, overpaid quarterback many believed should be relegated to backup duty. In a narrow football sense, he has become something far stranger: the quarterback booed by his own fans, belittled publicly by his owner, mocked by the press, and still standing. It is early, and the skepticism is earned. Still, Watson is quietly crafting one of the most improbable comeback stories in sports.

articles.title: Stuck between superpowers: How Australia navigates the China-US rivalry
articles.summary: Australia is increasingly concerned about China's military might - but Beijing is also its biggest trade partner.
articles.body:
Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead.

Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might.

" We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan.

"Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important."

War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation.

With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific , there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower.

But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner .

It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight.

"We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is.

The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific.

"We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says.

And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500.

A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing.

"Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said.

"China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects."

The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers.

But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties.

The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer.

But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US.

"Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll.

"Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States."

While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China.

Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner.

Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer.

Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015.

The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs.

And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up.

A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years.

Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges.

In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement.

Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary.

"There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments," says Lyons-Jones.

This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US.

Earlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be".

Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing.

"The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says.

But old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump , the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one.

"This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang.

And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act.

"There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says.

"It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

articles.title: Russia's foreign minister Sergey Lavrov questions UK's future
articles.summary: In response, Plaid Cymru said Wales' future was "not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit".
articles.body:
Russia's foreign minister has questioned the future of the UK, suggesting it looks uncertain with "the Celts" looking to hold independence referendums.

Sergey Lavrov made the comments at a youth conference where he said he did "not know what will become of the country called Great Britain", according to The Times .

The comments come weeks after the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland declared "Westminster's time is coming to an end" and signed an agreement to say it had no right to "block democracy".

In response to Lavrov's comments, Plaid Cymru said Wales' constitutional future was "a matter for the people of Wales", and "not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit".

In the conference, Lavrov also suggested the west had too much influence in the UN Security Council - the five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the UK, and the US.

According to The Times, he said: "The Celts — Wales, Ireland, Scotland — are now seeking to hold referenda.

"We do not advocate the expulsion of any of the permanent members of the security council. Although, of course, the scale of the British Empire, when it first took its seat in the UN security council at the organisation's founding, has, naturally, diminished to the utmost degree."

Plaid Cymru won a historic Senedd election victory in May, which means for the first time the biggest party in each devolved parliament is pro-independence.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth has declined to give a timetable for a referendum.

Former diplomat Craig Murray, who was jailed over blog posts he wrote about the trial of Alex Salmond in 2021, attended the international youth festival in Yekaterinburg after revealing he had been flown to the city by the Russian state.

In his blog, he said the meeting between the first ministers had been "featured with striking prominence" in Russian media.

Ap Iorwerth said last weekend there was "no turning back" on the independence journey, as he became the first leader of Wales to attend a Yes Cymru march.

In response to Lavrov's comments, a Plaid spokesman described Russia as an "existential threat to modern democracy".

"Plaid Cymru believes firmly in the right of nations to determine their own future through democratic means. That applies to Wales, and it applies to Ukraine," the spokesman said, referring to Russia's full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.

They said the memorandum with the SNP and Sinn Féin was about "strengthening democracy, cooperation, and standing up for the interests of our nations and communities".

"Wales' constitutional future is a matter for the people of Wales, and it is not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit," the statement added.

Stephen Gethins, the SNP's external affairs minister who had sanctions imposed on him by Russia, said: "The Scottish Government is committed to ensuring the people of Scotland have the democratic right to decide their constitutional future, just as we support the people of Ukraine and elsewhere in democratic Europe determining their future too."

articles.title: American and six Ukrainians released by India after six months in jail
articles.summary: Matthew VanDyke and six Ukrainians were accused of smuggling weapons and drones to armed ethnic groups fighting India.
articles.body:
Matthew VanDyke, a United States citizen held in India for more than six months and accused of supporting ethnic separatist groups, has been temporarily released on bail and returned to the US.

The 47-year-old arrived on Saturday morning and reunited with his family, according to a family spokesperson.

VanDyke, who runs a Washington, DC-based consultancy that says it provides “free security consulting, training, supplies and other services to vulnerable populations”, was detained in March by Indian authorities, along with six Ukrainian nationals who were also released on Saturday.

India’s main opposition Congress party said that, despite being “accused of plotting terrorist acts”, VanDyke was allowed to return home from New Delhi.

“Obviously US pressure determined this outcome, but what did India get in return?” Jairam Ramesh, a legislator and spokesperson for the party, posted on X.

VanDyke’s family told Al Jazeera before his release that his health was failing and he had lost weight after going on a month-long hunger strike in Tihar Jail to try to improve conditions in prison. He had to use a wheelchair to attend hearings, according to his mother, Sharon. VanDyke denied the accusations against him, and his family said he was in the region documenting the situation faced by minority ethnic groups.

Earlier this month, Indian prosecutors declined to bring terrorism charges against VanDyke and the others. Instead, prosecutors formally accused them of visa violations for entering restricted areas along the Myanmar border.

The Maryland native is a former filmmaker and rebel fighter during the Arab Spring and spent about six months in a Libyan prison during the Muammar Gaddafi regime. He was held alongside James Foley, a journalist who was later killed by ISIL in Syria. In recent years, VanDyke was based in Ukraine, where his consultancy helped train Ukrainian military forces.

In a statement to Al Jazeera before VanDyke’s release, James Foley’s mother, Diane, who now heads a foundation named after him, said she was “deeply saddened by his arrest in India and by his apparent poor health.” She added that her foundation called for “his release on humanitarian grounds.”

articles.title: Moms for Liberty co-founder warns parents about Ms Rachel’s political activism, ‘Not Mr Rogers’
articles.summary: Ms. Rachel's 21 million YouTube followers may not realize the children's entertainer has waded into political activism, says Moms for Liberty.
articles.body: Parents may think they are turning on Ms. Rachel for songs, speech lessons and early learning, but the co-founder of parental rights organization Moms for Liberty says they are increasingly exposing their toddlers to political activism. "She’s using her leadership role for political activism," Tina Descovich, the co-founder of Moms for Liberty, told Fox News Digital. Ms. Rachel, whose real name is Rachel Griffin Accurso, has more than 21 million YouTube followers and millions more across Instagram and TikTok. She has become increasingly outspoken on political issues, including the Israel-Gaza war, immigration detention and LGBTQ rights. MS RACHEL CLAIMS CELEBRITIES SILENT ON GAZA WOULD ‘PROBABLY’ SPEAK IF CHILDREN ‘WERE WHITE’ In December, Ms. Rachel was named as a finalist for StopAntisemitism’s 2025 "Antisemite of the Year" designation after the group accused her of promoting Hamas-aligned messaging in posts about Gaza. Other Jewish organizations have defended or supported her advocacy for Palestinian children. Descovich said parents turn to Ms. Rachel and expect educational programming that will help their children learn to speak, read and prepare for school. MS RACHEL DEFENDS HER ACTIVISM BY POINTING TO MISTER ROGERS' POLITICAL LEGACY ON CHILDREN'S TV "She reaches 21 million viewers a year on YouTube alone, and then her social media channels have, like Instagram, I think has five million, TikTok, 10 million, and she seems to think she can divide her personal views from her influence over toddlers, but parents are tuning in to her messaging because they trust her with their toddlers, and I think her shows should all start with a warning label that says, ‘Warning, this woman has been nominated to be the antisemite of the Year in the United States,’ and they should know that before they put her in front of their toddlers," Descovich said. Instead, she said, parents may now encounter political messaging involving gender identity, immigration and the Israel-Gaza conflict. MS RACHEL POSTS SUPPORT FOR HIJAB-WEARING KINDERGARTNERS AFTER TRUMP POST "Parents turn to her to teach their children potentially to be kind and be a good citizen and love your neighbor," Descovich said. "It would be great if she would teach kids the beginnings of learning to read and concepts so that they can be ready for kindergarten, but infiltrating gender ideology with children as young as two and three and four, that's not something parents are expecting or want to put in front of their kids at such a young age." In June, Ms. Rachel visited an immigration detention facility in Newark, N.J., called Delaney Hall to be with families she said had been "terrorized" by immigration enforcement. articles.title: FBI puts gangster Goldy Brar on Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially placed notorious gangster Satinderjeet Singh aka Goldy Brar, on its famed Ten Most Wanted
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has officially placed notorious gangster Satinderjeet Singh aka Goldy Brar, on its famed Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, offering a reward of up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest.The announcement, made early Tuesday, by the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, marks a major escalation in international law enforcement efforts targeting transnational crime syndicates operating across North America and Asia.Brar, who becomes the 543rd fugitive added to the historic list, faces multiple federal indictments in the United States, including Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) conspiracy, extortion, and narcotics trafficking.According to federal prosecutors, the fugitive serves as the primary North American operational leader for the Lawrence Bishnoi Organized Crime Group. Operating from a prison cell in India via contraband communications, Bishnoi allegedly delegated international operations to trusted lieutenants like Brar.The syndicate has been linked to a trail of violence across North America, including targeted assassinations, kidnappings, armed extortions, and large-scale drug smuggling—including the theft of over 500 kilograms of cocaine from rival cartels in the Los Angeles region.Among the most high-profile offenses detailed in federal court documents is the June 2023 assassination of prominent political and religious figure "H.S.N." outside a Sikh temple in Surrey, British Columbia.Bishnoi and Brar are charged with ordering the targeted killing. Canadian authorities subsequently designated the Bishnoi syndicate as a terrorist entity in September 2025, highlighting its routine use of public violence and social media threat campaigns to extort individuals within Indian diaspora communities worldwide.Brar’s inclusion on the Top Ten list stems from "Operation Hardball," a years-long multi-agency investigation that unsealed indictments against 37 defendants connected to India-based transnational crime groups in July 2026. While 28 defendants have been taken into custody or located, five key fugitives remain at large alongside Brar.Law enforcement leaders from the FBI, the Los Angeles Police Department, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) emphasized that placing Brar on the global list ensures his face will be publicized worldwide until he is captured.Considered armed, extremely violent, and dangerous, Brar is believed to be hiding in parts of California or Canada. articles.title: Myanmar army air strike kills dozens in Rakhine state
articles.summary: Nearly half a million people are displaced in Rakhine as a result of the conflict between the military and rebel groups.
articles.body:
An air strike carried out by Myanmar’s military has killed at least 33 people in territory controlled by rebel factions.

The attack near a market in the north of the Rakhine state in the west of the country on Monday also wounded 36 people, rescue and rebel group officials reported. The strikes are the latest in a series of assaults against pro-democracy and ethnic armed groups by the military government, which took power in a coup in 2021, sparking armed opposition.

The Arakan army said a fighter jet dropped two bombs near a local market in the town of Kyauktaw at noon local time (0530 GMT), killing 33 people, including vendors, shoppers, and pedestrians. It said the death toll “may continue to increase”.

Wai Hun Aung, a senior rescue official in Rakhine, confirmed the details to the Associated Press news agency. He said the market was the region’s main wholesale centre, drawing traders and shoppers from across the state.

“This is one of the most severe airstrikes in Rakhine,” he said. Photos and videos posted on social media showed buildings on fire, damaged vehicles and parts of a nearby bridge destroyed.

Myanmar’s military did not immediately comment, but it has previously said it strikes only legitimate military targets and accused resistance groups of “terrorism”.

Myanmar has been gripped by ⁠conflict since the elected ⁠government led by Aung San Suu Kyi was ousted in the 2021 coup. A nationwide resistance movement has since evolved into a civil war between the ‌military government and an array of armed ethnic and pro-democracy groups.

President Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s former military government chief, was elected by ‌a military-backed Parliament in April, formalising his grip on power after five years of army rule.

The Arakan army is a well-trained and well-armed military group seeking autonomy for Rakhine’s ethnic minority. It launched an offensive in November 2023 and has since captured strategically important military headquarters and 14 of the state’s 17 townships.

The military has imposed severe restrictions on trade routes to Rakhine since the fighting there intensified, worsening food shortages.

In December, a military airstrike on a hospital in Rakhine’s Mrauk U township killed at least 33 people and wounded 70 others.

Nearly half a million people are displaced in Rakhine as a result of the conflict, according to United Nations data. The UN added in August that the human rights situation in Myanmar has plummeted “to a new low”, citing “brutal abuse” against the Rohingya minority and the devastating impact of illicit economic activity, including illegal mining for rare earth minerals.

Rebel groups and Myanmar’s military are now both using drones in the protracted conflict, which has killed more than 100,000 people, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project.

articles.title: Cyber fraud money routed via 903 gaming accounts
articles.summary: Lucknow cyber police probe Rs 95.65 lakh digital-arrest scam; funds routed via 2 bank accounts then split across 903 gaming accounts; Rs 44 lakh frozen.
articles.body: Lucknow: Cyber fraudsters are increasingly using online gaming accounts and digital wallets to disperse and conceal money siphoned from victims, creating a new challenge for investigators tracking financial trails. The trend emerged during a probe into a Rs 95.65 lakh digital-arrest fraud registered at Lucknow’s Cyber Crime Police Station on Sept 25.According to ADCP (Crime) Kiran Yadav, fraudsters posing as CBI and ED officials threatened the victim through WhatsApp calls and video conferencing, claiming links to a money-laundering case and impending arrest. Under pressure, the victim transferred Rs 95.65 lakh.Police have so far secured around Rs 44 lakh by placing liens on suspect accounts. Financial analysis revealed that the money was first routed through two primary bank accounts in Guwahati and Ranchi before being distributed across 903 online gaming accounts.Police said cybercriminals increasingly avoid transferring large amounts directly, instead splitting the proceeds into smaller transactions routed through multiple bank accounts, gaming wallets and digital platforms. articles.title: In a relatively mild speech, North Korea uses UN platform to lament ‘mutual distrust’ and tension
articles.summary: North Korea used its yearly U.N. platform on Monday to warn other world leaders of “a harsh reality rampant with unprecedented mutual distrust and confrontation,” but said that it would endure and, in a multilateral world, “surely attain all that we plan to, relying entirely on our own efforts.”
articles.body: North Korea used its yearly U.N. platform on Monday to warn other world leaders of “a harsh reality rampant with unprecedented mutual distrust and confrontation,” but said that it would endure and, in a multilateral world, “surely attain all that we plan to, relying entirely on our own efforts.” It was, by Pyongyang’s standards, a relatively mild speech that contained no direct threats. The annual opportunity for the country, whose formal name is the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, to speak on the world stage fell this year to Vice Foreign Minister Kim Son Gyong. Like many nations, he touted the notion of U.N.-focused multilateralism, yet repeatedly insisted that North Korea could — and would, if necessary — go it alone. “Gone are the days when an individual member state unilaterally imposed its will on the rest of the world and dominated the international political arena,” Kim said. “Instead, multilateralism and multipolarization have emerged as an irresistible aspiration and trend of the times based on justice and equity.” North Korea is frequently at odds with South Korea, Japan and the United States, which are tightly aligned in matters of security in East Asia. Kim asserted once again that his nation, no matter the external threat, is prepared to defend itself. “No physical conflict has occurred on and around the Korean Peninsula, a hot spot of the world, and the security index is being maintained at a higher level than any other part of the globe,” he said. “We owe it to the fact that the DPRK has a war deterrent in place powerful enough to break anyone’s will to start a war of aggression against the DPRK and that we are thoroughly containing and managing the hostile forces’ intention to use force.” A range of remarks across subjects As is typical for North Korean speeches at the U.N. — and, for that matter, for many nations’ speeches — Kim’s remarks ranged across the nation’s priorities and goals, with special emphasis on its ability to defend itself in a volatile security situation in East Asia. A sampling: — On Japan: “An A-class war criminal.” — On the regional balance of power in East Asia: “maintained by the DPRK’s self-defensive capabilities.” — On the United Nations itself: “The organization still fails to recover from functional paralysis owing to the high-handedness and unilateralism of a handful of countries pursuing only chauvinistic interests.” — On nuclear weapons: “The DPRK’s nuclear deterrent is the absolute might and irresistible force designed, from A to Z, to safeguard the sovereignty, security and peace against aggression and threat from outside.” “The DPRK will continue to strictly control and manage every external threat by dint of her supremacy in overwhelming strength,” Kim said. Intense rhetoric is a hallmark of North Korea North Korea’s rhetoric is often overheated and its criticism of rivals often over the top. Monday was no exception. What seemed noteworthy, though, was how pro forma it felt: There were no threats of anything that might destabilize the region or cause other nations from Japan to South Korea to the United States to brace for any specific moves. Saying that “a more offensive and aggressive military bloc with a nuclear element” and its activities have provoked North Korea and destabilized the Korean Peninsula, Kim condemned what he framed as the collusion of Tokyo, Seoul and Washington against Pyongyang. He made no mention of North Korea’s role in tensions on the peninsula, including sporadic missile launches that send its rivals scrambling. Two days before the U.N. meeting in which he was speaking began, North Korea launched two short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea, days after it threatened to bolster its nuclear deterrent capabilities. Kim is a relatively mid-level official in leader Kim Jong Un’s third-generation government, and thus spoke as one of the final speakers of the final day of the leaders’ meeting, or General Debate. The Korean Peninsula split in two after North Korea and South Korea fought a bloody war from 1950 to 1953, backed by China and the United States, respectively. Though an armistice was eventually signed, the two countries remain in a technical state of war, and the border between them is guarded by a heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone.

articles.title: Crop-loss panchanamas across Maharashtra from today, says agriculture minister
articles.summary: Maharashtra to start crop-loss panchanamas Tuesday after kharif damage from rainfall gaps; opposition and farmers demand immediate relief and fodder camps.
articles.body: Pune: Crop-loss panchanamas will begin across Maharashtra from Tuesday following widespread damage to kharif yields caused by prolonged gaps in rainfall, state agriculture minister Dattatray Bharne said on Monday.“State govt is supporting farmers and will provide all help. The panchanama is a mandatory procedure that we have to undertake. However, our intention is to help every affected farmer. The state is also planning fodder camps in the drought-affected regions to protect livestock,” he told the media in the city.Opposition netas Rohit Pawar and Rajesh Tope, however, demanded immediate relief for farmers, arguing that panchanamas were unnecessary in areas where crops had suffered complete loss. They urged the state to provide blanket assistance without waiting for the formal assessment process.“The immediate relief to farmers should be the first and foremost task for govt. It should be extended before Diwali so that they can sustain themselves during the coming rabi season,” said NCP’s Pawar who represents Karjat-Jamkhed in the Assembly. Pawar has been touring the affected districts in Vidarbha and Marathwada for the last two weeks.Farmers and activists said the situation was worsening as cultivators faced losses after spending heavily on seeds, fertilisers and cultivation. They also called for immediate arrangements for fodder and water for livestock.“In many fields, there is nothing left to assess. Crops have completely dried up and we need immediate financial assistance,” said farmer activist Shantaram Sarvade from Khed tehsil.“Our crops have failed, but our cattle still need fodder. Fodder camps should start immediately,” said an affected farmer.Farmers in eight drought-affected tehsils of Pune district also want immediate panchanamas of their crops. “We do not know when this process is going to begin. If they do it early, they would be able to assess the ground situation early. Otherwise, they would not properly understand the losses,” said Sarika Ingle, a farmer from Shirur tehsil. Shirur has so far experienced a rainfall gap of 51 days.“There is hardly anything left to assess in many fields. The crop has dried up and the money we spent on seeds, fertilisers and cultivation has already been lost,” said Santosh Kolpe from Daund tehsil.Farmers’ activists said assistance needed to reach cultivators before they were pushed further into debt. They urged govt to use available field-level information to provide interim relief while completing the formal assessment required for compensation and other schemes.Vaibhav Tambe, district agriculture officer, told TOI, “We will initiate panchanamas of the affected fields on Tuesday.
